It seems to us that this major strength of Aristotelian logic found a particularly receptive audience within Arab-Islamic thought.
That is why it gained an important place and influenced many of the processes taking place as Arab-Islamic thought developed historically.

We mean the rise of Arab-Islamic science, followed by the rise of philosophical inquiry into religious belief, nature, and society. This development moved at a remarkably rapid pace. In less than roughly a century, and through kalām, it moved from a mainly theological direction toward philosophical systems that achieved a considerable degree of independence from theology.
We do not mean to give Aristotelian logic a larger place in the history of medieval Arab-Islamic thought than it really had.
Our aim is simply to recognize its real importance without either minimizing or exaggerating it.
That brings us to several materialist elements in Aristotle’s logic that some Arab thinkers of the period were able to recognize.
The first appears in Aristotle’s Categories, in his discussion of knowledge and the object of knowledge.

Here Aristotle takes what can be called a materialist position. He argues that the object we know must exist before our knowledge of it. Knowledge can arise only if there is first something there to be known.
He says that knowledge and the object of knowledge do not necessarily come into existence at the same time.
If the object of knowledge disappears, then knowledge of it must also disappear. But the disappearance of our knowledge does not necessarily mean that the object itself disappears.
Take, for example, the squaring of the circle. Knowledge of it does not yet exist, Aristotle says, but the squaring of the circle still exists as something that could potentially be known.
In this idea, Aristotle accepts the priority of what exists over consciousness. On this particular question, then, he takes a materialist position.
There is another part of Aristotle’s logic that also expresses a materialist position.

When Aristotle discusses the concept, or essence, he argues that the universal is not some separate spiritual reality existing beyond individual things or beyond the material world, as it is in Plato’s world of Forms.
Instead, the universal exists within particulars—the general within the particular.
The universal cannot exist without individual things. Nor can we come to know a universal without first encountering individual things repeatedly.

There is, however, a difference between knowing an individual thing and knowing the universal concept. We know the individual through the senses. We know the universal through reason, by mental abstraction.
Aristotle’s understanding of the relationship between concepts and reality therefore also represents a materialist position.

Because of these and similar features in Aristotle’s logic, and because major Arab-Islamic thinkers were able to recognize them, Aristotelian logic could play the positive and progressive role we have described.
It did so in three main ways.
First, it helped the scientific tendency mature within the wider cultural activity of Arab-Islamic society.
Second, it provided an effective way of directing productive intellectual abilities toward mental abstraction—in other words, toward moving thought from simpler to more complex forms.
Third, Aristotle’s logic helped strengthen the rationalist current that led the intellectual and ideological opposition to the idea that knowledge had only one source: a supernatural one.
The positive features of Aristotle’s logic were visible to all the major intellectual and ideological currents of the period.
Their attitudes toward it therefore differed according to their wider intellectual and ideological positions.
A — The Position of the Extreme Traditionalist Current
This current took a hostile position toward Aristotle’s logic and philosophy for both religious and social reasons.
It attacked them fiercely, persecuted those who studied them, and encouraged their persecution in the name of religion.

Hostility toward Aristotelian logic and philosophy began to become especially visible after the Abbasid caliph al-Mutawakkil came to power in 232 AH/846 CE and began persecuting the Muʿtazila and their doctrine.
But the larger wave of hostility toward philosophy and logic came later, with the campaign of intellectual terror led by theologians and Ashʿarites.
They themselves used the methods of logic, but mainly in its rigid and purely formal form.
The most famous Ashʿarite scholar, and the one who had the greatest influence on religious public opinion, was Abū Ḥāmid al-Ghazālī (1059–1111). He became the leading figure in this campaign.
For generations afterward, his thought continued to cast a shadow of fear over philosophy and philosophers.
This influence reached every region in which Arab-Islamic intellectual life was active, in both the eastern and western Islamic worlds. But its weight appears to have been even greater in the West.

This may have been connected with the dominance there of the Mālikī school of law, which had a particularly conservative and traditionalist character and placed especially strong emphasis on inherited texts.
The rulers of the ṭāʾifa kingdoms, princes, and other political authorities in al-Andalus and North Africa made use of the influence enjoyed by Muslim theologians.

They needed the support of religious scholars who held great intellectual influence over public opinion, while those religious figures in turn supported rulers in suppressing free thought, which at the time was represented above all by philosophy and logic.

Books and entire libraries were burned more than once. Thinkers were imprisoned, exiled, persecuted, or stoned after rigid and reactionary jurists stirred rulers and the public against anyone they suspected of departing from their traditionalist way of thinking through an interest in philosophy or logic.
One Andalusian thinker of the period described this historical reality as follows:

“I saw the art of logic rejected among them and cast aside. They paid it no attention and gave it no importance. More than this, the people of our time recoil from it and accuse anyone learned in it of heresy and unbelief.”
The wave of intellectual terror associated with al-Ghazālī weakened for a time with the appearance of Ibn Rushd, the great philosopher of the Islamic West.
Ibn Rushd defended philosophy and directly attacked al-Ghazālī’s hostility toward it. He wrote The Incoherence of the Incoherence in reply to al-Ghazālī’s The Incoherence of the Philosophers.
But Ibn Rushd was able to lift this dark shadow from philosophical thought only briefly.
Before long, it descended on Ibn Rushd himself, despite his high scientific and social standing throughout al-Andalus and the Islamic West.
Muslim theologians turned the ruler of the country against him, claiming that he had written works showing corruption in his religion and beliefs.
The great philosopher was put on trial before the ruling prince in the presence of leading theologians who held enormous influence over the religious thinking of the Muslim population.
He was sentenced to exile. A number of other free-thinking intellectuals of his time were punished with him.
The punishment was lifted only shortly before Ibn Rushd died in 1198.
After Ibn Rushd, the wave of intellectual repression associated with al-Ghazālī again came to dominate philosophical thought almost completely, and its creative movement stagnated.
During the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, the pressure became even heavier. Hostility toward philosophy and logic was one of the dominant features of the period.
The young philosopher and mystic Shihāb al-Dīn al-Suhrawardī had already been killed near the end of the twelfth century, in 587 AH/1191 CE, after being accused of philosophy and unbelief.
After him came two major leaders of rigid traditionalist religious thought who expressed the hostility of conservative forces toward logic and philosophy in particularly aggressive language.
The first was Abū ʿAmr Taqī al-Dīn al-Shahrazūrī, better known as Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ (d. 643 AH/c. 1244 CE).
The second was the figure known as Shaykh al-Islām Ibn Taymiyya (d. 728 AH/1328 CE).
Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ issued the famous ruling known historically as the “Fatwa of Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ,” which prohibited both teaching and studying logic and philosophy.
“…As for logic, it is the gateway to philosophy, and the gateway to evil is itself evil.”

From these premises he went on to support harsh action against those who studied philosophy and logic. He called for their persecution in every area of life, even for cutting off their means of livelihood and depriving them of life itself.
Ibn Taymiyya waged a similar war against philosophical thought.

He prohibited the reading of books by philosophers and logicians, accused Ibn Sīnā of teaching union with God in his Majmūʿat al-Rasāʾil al-Kubrā (Cairo edition, p. 138), and wrote a separate work attacking the views of theologians, logicians, philosophers, and Sufis.
In the fourteenth century, the religious leader known as Imam al-Dhahabī followed the same path.
He declared that there was no “remedy for the sciences of philosophy, or for those who carry and practice them, except burning and removing them from existence.”
Sectarian intolerance and intellectual rigidity alone do not explain this hostility toward logic.
Behind both, we need to look for something deeper.
We need to ask about the social position of these intolerant thinkers and the ideological basis of their attitudes.
Conservative jurists undoubtedly understood how strongly Aristotle’s logic could help philosophical thought develop and how it could bring out materialist positions among some philosophical thinkers.
B — The Traditionalist Current That Made Use of Aristotelian Logic
This hostility toward Aristotle’s logic does not mean that every traditionalist opposed it in exactly the same way.
Nor does it mean that they avoided using logic in their own theological writings or escaped its influence on their own methods of thought.

In reality, the influence of logic had become too deep and too firmly established for anyone working seriously in questions of thought or science—whatever kind of science—to remain completely outside it, regardless of their intellectual or ideological position.
For that reason, especially among later traditionalists, we find another form of hostility toward Aristotle’s logic.
It differed from the open and rigid hostility described in the previous section.
These thinkers separated Aristotle’s logic from its substantive meaning—from its relation to knowledge—and reduced it to one aspect alone: pure form.
The great social philosopher Ibn Khaldūn clearly recognized this kind of “change” in Aristotle’s logic, as he called it.

After reviewing the contents of Aristotle’s eight logical works, discussing their translation “within the Islamic community,” and describing how Muslim philosophers circulated them through commentaries and summaries, Ibn Khaldūn wrote:
“…Then the later scholars came and changed the terminology of logic.”
He then identified the exact point where this change had taken place:

“…They discussed the syllogism only in terms of its general ability to produce conclusions, without regard to its subject matter. They removed the study of the syllogism according to its material content—that is, the five books on Demonstration, Dialectic, Rhetoric, Poetics, and Sophistics. Some of them may touch on a little of this, but only briefly. They neglected these works almost as though they did not exist, even though they are the most important and essential part of the discipline.”
Whatever position this group of traditionalists took toward Aristotle’s logic, they still used it, even in their attacks on philosophy and philosophers.
They used mainly its purely formal side.
Al-Ghazālī himself is the clearest example.

Despite his famous hostility toward philosophy and philosophers and his historical campaign against them, he not only wrote several works devoted specifically to formal logic. He also placed a purely logical introduction at the beginning of his al-Mustaṣfā.
There, in very firm language, he states that anyone who does not understand the logical questions covered in that introduction cannot be trusted in his knowledge.

Before al-Ghazālī, Imam al-Ḥaramayn, one of the leading early Ashʿarites (d. 478 AH), had already used Aristotelian logic in his discussions of the principles of Islamic law, despite disagreeing with parts of that logic.
Among later thinkers of this traditionalist current were Najm al-Dīn al-Rāzī (d. 606 AH/early thirteenth century) and Afḍal al-Dīn al-Khūnajī (d. 646 AH/mid-thirteenth century).
Both gave considerable attention to logic in their writings, but in the way Ibn Khaldūn described above.
The Andalusian thinker Ibn Ḥazm (d. 456 AH/c. 1064) took a similar position toward Aristotle’s logic.

Although his Ẓāhirī school made him a strict traditionalist, he defended logic and wrote the well-known work Approximation to the Limits of Logic and an Introduction to It through Everyday Examples and Juristic Expressions.
His book was, in practice, an answer to the hostility shown toward logic by the jurists and later theologians of his time.
